extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (novelists/short-story/YA) seeking guidance on writing Latinx characters and other-culture representation
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for creating believable, specific Latinx characters in fiction by researching cultural, regional, familial, linguistic, and intersectional details and avoiding broad/generalized portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latinx is not just one thing
rubrics_metrics.description: Latinx is a catchall term for people with Latin American heritage; there are very many different labels and experiences and "there’s no one right way and there’s no umbrella term."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating Latinx as monolithic. The page emphasizes that broad portrayals of a culture or group are likely to be misleading, while being specific about a culture or family can be very relatable. Examples: differences between Mexican, Cuban, Puerto Rican, Dominican, Central and South American experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific about origin, family, and upbringing
rubrics_metrics.description: To write a Latinx character, think about where they live, how they got there, what’s their family story, how did they grow up, what kind of foods do they eat and when.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide a specific country/region/state/city, immigration story (first generation, assimilated, diaspora), rural vs urban background, and family makeup — these details shape behavior and perspective. The hosts note that micro-cultures (e.g., within Mexico or within immigrant communities in the U.S.) matter. Anti-pattern: assuming a single 'Latinx' experience fits all characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use food and meal scenes as a gateway to cultural specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Food — traditional foods, comfort foods, and immigrant mashup foods — are key details that reveal culture, family history, and emotional associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write scenes centered on meals to show what comforts a character, what they miss, how they blend traditions (examples: ceviche, fish grilled in achiote, regional rice-and-beans variations, mashed potatoes as comfort food, immigrant ketchup anecdote). Consider when and how certain dishes are eaten (holiday vs everyday) and how foods may have fused in diaspora communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on intersectionality — multiple identity facets matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Intersectionality is the idea that everyone has more than one thing that informs their identity (e.g., Latinx and queer, Latinx and disabled).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember that ethnicity intersects with gender, sexuality, disability, class, religion, and more; those intersections produce uniquely different experiences. Use intersectional details to avoid one-dimensional characters and to explain why two Latinx characters may have divergent perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray code-switching and context-dependent behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: People 'code switch' — they act differently at school than at a grandmother’s house or in different social contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how characters shift language, tone, mannerisms, and behavior across contexts (family, public, workplace, among peers). This helps convey authenticity and the lived complexity of bicultural or immigrant experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research respectfully — talk to people and look up regional specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Talk to people (politely) about where they’re from and what their family customs and foods are; if someone tells you a region/town, look it up to learn details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical research tip: ask staff at ethnic restaurants where they’re from (without harassing them), then research the region’s cuisine and customs. Use interviews and lived accounts to find specific, concrete details. Anti-pattern: shallow or token research that only uses stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that you will make mistakes; treat mistakes as part of learning
rubrics_metrics.description: You will make mistakes, that’s part of the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to feedback and correction rather than expecting to be 100% perfect. Do the work, revise, and listen to responses from members of the community you depict. The hosts normalize errors while urging careful, specific portrayal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise about diaspora geography and local demographics
rubrics_metrics.description: Where in the U.S. (or other country) your character lives affects which Latin American communities they most likely interact with (e.g., South Florida — Cubans; New York — Puerto Ricans and Dominicans; California — Mexicans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use local demographic knowledge to make plausible social networks, food availability, language use, and cultural practices. This helps avoid mismatches between setting and character background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cultural mislabeling — match character background to intended audience/community
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t conflate Mexican experience with Mexican-American experience (or any other conflation); portraying a Mexican family may not resonate with Mexican-American readers if it ignores diasporic specificities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dan’s anecdote: portraying Mexican families did not read as Mexican-American to that audience. Decide whether your character’s experience is immigrant, first-generation, assimilated, or from the home country, and portray accordingly. Anti-pattern: using homeland details for diaspora characters without accounting for assimilation or hybridity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cultural artifacts and specific details to ground authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate specific cultural items and practices (e.g., Lotería cards, particular regional sauces, games or rituals) to root a story in a recognizable lived experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Guadalupe Garcia McCall’s use of Lotería in a Texas/Mexican-American story demonstrates specificity. Such artifacts should be used accurately and in context, showing how they matter to the characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight family dynamics where culturally appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: In many Latinx contexts family togetherness is emphasized; family relationships influence character choices and scenes (especially in YA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray family interactions realistically — family dinners, multi-generational households, obligations, and communal problem-solving. Use family-specific details to create relatable dynamics rather than sidelining families for plot convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage sensory detail and small concrete images
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensory details (taste, texture, smell) make cultural scenes vivid and emotionally resonant (e.g., black beans looking like 'chocolate pudding').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sensory metaphors and concrete descriptions to evoke comfort or dissonance. These details help readers from within the culture recognize authenticity and help outsiders empathize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of language and inclusive terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand terms like Latinx and their relationship to gendered forms in Spanish (Latino/Latina); pronunciation and acceptance vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inclusive terms thoughtfully and be aware of contested or regionally variable usages. If using Spanish, account for gendered grammar and community preferences; don't assume universal acceptance of any single label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice assignment: write a meal scene from a specific cultural POV
rubrics_metrics.description: Homework: research and then write a meal scene in the POV of a person from a specific culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exercise asks you to pick any meal (holiday, fast food, solo, fantasy/space setting allowed) and ground the scene in who the character is, where they’re from, how they feel about the food, and how it informs conversation or thoughts. This practice reinforces specificity, sensory detail, and intersectional context.
